lines.text: I do, as I say, love these books with all my heart--and I love you too.
lines.note: Robert's first direct declaration of love after praising Elizabeth's books.

lines.text: Sympathy is dear--very dear to me: but the sympathy of a poet, and of such a poet, is the quintessence of sympathy to me!
lines.note: Elizabeth answers that a poet's sympathy is the quintessence of sympathy to her.

lines.text: You will never more, I hope, talk of 'the honour of my acquaintance,' but I will joyfully wait for the delight of your friendship, and the spring, and my Chapel-sight after all!
lines.note: Robert looks ahead to spring, friendship, and seeing her at the chapel.

lines.text: This I will say, then--wait and know me better, as you will one long day at the end.
lines.note: Robert asks Elizabeth to know him better over a long day at the end.

lines.text: Well, but, I wanted particularly to say this--Don't bring the 'Duchess' with you on Wednesday.
lines.note: Elizabeth tells Robert not to bring the Duchess, showing their growing ease over his work.

lines.text: Pomegranates you may cut deep down the middle and see into, but not hearts,--so why should I try and speak?
lines.note: Robert's pomegranate image answers Elizabeth's wish to see into things.

lines.text: And now, my love--I am round you ... my whole life is wound up and down and over you....
lines.note: Robert's sweeping declaration that his whole life is wound around Elizabeth.

lines.text: You cannot guess what you are to me--you cannot--it is not possible:--and though I have said that before, I must say it again ... for it comes again to be said.
lines.note: Elizabeth says Robert is between her and even the closest graves.

lines.text: So I rest on you, for life, for death, beloved--beside you do stand, in my solemn belief, the direct miraculous gift of God to me--that is my solemn belief; may I be thankful!
lines.note: Robert rests his life and death on Elizabeth as God's gift.

lines.text: Every word you write goes to my heart and lives there: let us live so, and die so, if God will.
lines.note: Robert says every word Elizabeth writes goes to his heart and lives there.

lines.text: Ah, the chestnut tree: do you think that I never saw the chestnut tree before?
lines.note: Elizabeth recalls Robert's chestnut tree from his earlier letter.

lines.text: And you pretend not to know I would walk barefoot till I dropped, if so I might attain to the sight of you, and it.
lines.note: Robert says he would walk barefoot until he dropped to see Elizabeth.

lines.text: So my dear, own Ba has good sense, best sense—whatever Flush’s may be!
lines.note: Robert marvels that Ba has good sense, best sense.

lines.text: I would not say to you yesterday, perhaps could not, that you wrote ever so much foolishness to me in the morning, dearest, and that I knew it ever so well.
lines.note: Elizabeth says she would not say yesterday's foolishness and knew it well.
